concepts.label: Biodiversity and Why It Matters
concepts.cardText: The immense variety of living organisms on the Earth is known as biodiversity, and it is essential for life on the Earth. Every organism plays a role in keeping nature stable and functioning: microscopic algae in the oceans release most of the oxygen we breathe, fungi and bacteria decompose fallen leaves and convert waste into manure making the soil fertile, birds, bees and bats pollinate flowers, and plants capture sunlight to prepare food that supports nearly all life. Humans depend on biodiversity for food, shelter, medicines and livelihoods. For centuries farmers conserved diverse crop varieties with useful characteristics, realising that diversity reduces the risk of crop failure and strengthens food security. To study diversity systematically, scientists group and classify organisms based on their shared characteristics and evolutionary relationships.

concepts.label: India as a Biodiversity Hotspot
concepts.cardText: India's natural landscape is diverse, with mountains in the north, desert in the west, rainforests in the North East, plateaus in the south and long coastlines, each with distinct soil types and climatic conditions. These diverse habitats together support a wide variety of species. Some species are restricted to particular regions of the world and are not found naturally anywhere else; such species are called endemic species, for example the Nilgiri tahr, the Lion-tailed macaque, the Indian pitcher plant Nepenthes khasiana and Neelakurinji, which are found only in India. Regions that support a large number of endemic species and have undergone significant habitat loss are known as biodiversity hotspots, and they are particularly important for conservation. The Western Ghats, Indo-Burma (including North East India), the Himalayas and Sundaland (including the Nicobar Islands) are examples of global biodiversity hotspots. Protecting these regions is important as they support food webs and help ecosystems remain healthy.

concepts.label: How Biodiversity Has Evolved
concepts.cardText: The biodiversity that we see today was not always the same. Small differences among individuals affected their chances of survival and reproduction by helping them adapt to changed conditions. These differences accumulated over many generations and gave rise to new forms of life. The diversity we see today is therefore an outcome of continuous changes occurring over a vast span of time, shaped by interactions between organisms and their surroundings. The study of this biological diversity is possible through a systematic framework that is provided by classification. Some ancient Indian traditions, such as the Sangam Tinai classification of landscapes and the protection of sacred groves, show a sophisticated understanding of landscapes and their biota and effectively preserved locally diverse habitats.

concepts.label: Criteria for Classifying Living Organisms
concepts.cardText: The same organism can fit into different groups depending on the criterion chosen. Scientists often look at broad and easily visible features and then at more detailed features. The criteria they use include external features such as shape, size and body organisation; mode of nutrition, autotrophic or heterotrophic; internal structures such as skeletal patterns, presence or absence of organs and different types of tissues; cell structure, whether unicellular or multicellular, eukaryote or prokaryote, with or without a cell wall; ecological role as producer, consumer or decomposer; reproduction by asexual and/or sexual methods; and genetic similarity, studied in detail using DNA. These features help in understanding similarities and differences among organisms. Similar features in organisms suggest that they have evolved from common ancestors.

concepts.label: The Need for Biological Classification
concepts.cardText: Imagine thousands of books scattered on the floor of a library: without arranging them into subjects, authors or sections, finding any book would be difficult. In the same way, the Earth is home to millions of organisms, so classifying them systematically helps us in understanding them better. The Pakke Tiger Reserve in Arunachal Pradesh has nearly 300 recorded bird species, including four hornbill species found in different parts of the forest depending on tree size and fruit availability. To make the study of such vast diversity easier, scientists group organisms based on their similarities and/or differences. This scientific system of grouping living organisms is known as biological classification. It makes the study of living organisms more organised and systematic; helps us understand similarities and differences among living beings and how they are related and interact; helps in identifying and naming newly discovered organisms; supports biodiversity conservation by identifying organisms under threat of extinction; and allows scientists all over the world to discuss organisms using a common system.

concepts.label: Classification Systems Over Time
concepts.cardText: Scientists have developed different classification systems over time, based on the knowledge available. Aristotle, around the 4th century BCE, grouped animals based on their habitat (land, water and air) and external appearances, but this system had limitations because it relied mainly on easily observable external characteristics. In the 18th century the two kingdom system divided all living organisms into Plantae, organisms that do not move and synthesise their own food, and Animalia, organisms that move and depend on other organisms for food. This created confusion for organisms like Amoeba, Paramecium and bacteria, so a third kingdom, Protista, was added for unicellular microscopic organisms. As microscopes improved, scientists noticed an amoeba has a true nucleus but bacteria do not, so bacteria were placed in a separate kingdom, Monera, giving a four kingdom system. Later, fungi such as mushrooms, which do not move like plants but are heterotrophic and obtain nutrients by absorption, were placed in a separate kingdom, giving the five kingdom classification of Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.

concepts.label: Five Kingdom Classification: Criteria
concepts.cardText: In the five kingdom classification all life forms are grouped based on certain common features. The criteria are cell type (prokaryote or eukaryote), cell structure (presence or absence of a cell wall), level of organisation (unicellular or multicellular) and mode of nutrition (autotrophic or heterotrophic). Scientists classify organisms based on the cell structure, number of cells, mode of nutrition and the organism's ecological role. Whittaker's five kingdom classification system, Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia, is a simple and useful system to understand diversity. It offered a more comprehensive way to group organisms than the previous systems, but it still could not fully explain the diversity of life. Viruses, which contain genetic material but lack cellular organisation, do not fit into any of the five kingdoms.

concepts.label: Kingdom Monera
concepts.cardText: Bacteria and cyanobacteria are single-celled prokaryotes that are grouped under Monera. Bacteria are found everywhere, including soil, water, air, hot springs and other extreme environments where most organisms cannot survive, and they are present even inside the human body. They are also found in the gut of ruminants and are responsible for the production of biogas from the dung of these animals. Some bacteria are harmful pathogens and cause diseases but many are useful, like Lactobacillus and Rhizobium. In addition to nutrient cycling, some bacteria also break down pollutants like oil, pesticides and sewage. Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) were among the first organisms to produce oxygen through photosynthesis; about 2.5 billion years ago oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere, making the Earth suitable for other forms of life.

concepts.label: Kingdom Fungi
concepts.cardText: Fungi are mostly multicellular eukaryotes with cell walls made of chitin. They do not make their own food; they absorb nutrients from dead or decaying matter through fine filaments which together form a network known as mycelium. Most fungi are saprophytes and play a very important ecological role as decomposers, feeding on dead organic matter such as fallen leaves, twigs or dead organisms and breaking down complex organic matter into simpler substances that become available in the soil as minerals. Some fungi establish a mutualistic (symbiotic) relationship with other organisms while others live as parasites and cause diseases in plants and animals. They reproduce both sexually and asexually, often by forming spores, and grow best in warm and moist conditions. Yeast and Aspergillus mould are common fungi; although yeast is unicellular, its cell wall is made of chitin, so it is put under fungi. Mushrooms are macroscopic fungi that reproduce by spores. Without fungi the decay of dead plants and animals would be greatly reduced, adversely affecting soil fertility and ecological balance.

concepts.label: Kingdom Plantae and Thallophyta
concepts.cardText: Plants are multicellular, autotrophic organisms that perform photosynthesis. Their cells have a rigid cell wall primarily made of cellulose, which provides support and protection. All plants belong to the kingdom Plantae. Plants form the base of most of the food chains and release oxygen which is essential for life on the Earth. The kingdom Plantae is further divided into five classes: Thallophyta, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta, Gymnosperm and Angiosperm. Thallophytes are among the simplest plant forms and are mostly found in water or moist environments. They form a thallus, a simple body that allows direct exchange of gases, nutrients and water with the surroundings. They are well-adapted to aquatic habitats, an example being Spirogyra.

concepts.label: Lichens: Symbiosis and Bioindicators
concepts.cardText: White-green patches on tree trunks, damp walls or stones are lichens, which villagers recognise as an indicator of a pollution-free environment. Lichens change their colour with air pollutants, and based on their colour researchers can find out the concentration of pollutants in the air, so they are natural bioindicators for the measurement of air quality. Biologically they are symbiotic, a mutual association of two organisms: one partner is an autotrophic alga and the other is a heterotrophic fungus. The fungal partner provides protection, and the algal partner photosynthesises and provides food. Some lichens are used as a spice, medicines and dyes, but some are poisonous, so it is important to classify and identify them properly for safe and proper utilisation.

concepts.label: Bryophyta: Amphibians of the Plant Kingdom
concepts.cardText: Bryophytes, such as mosses and liverworts, represent an important shift from water to land. Bryophytes survive in moist and shady places, growing as green mats on the soil, especially during the monsoons. They require water for reproduction, so they are called the amphibians of the plant kingdom. They show how plants began to colonise land while remaining dependent on moisture. Examples are Marchantia and moss.

concepts.label: Angiosperms: Flowers, Fruits and Dispersal

These features allow angiosperms to occupy a wide range of environments, so they are the most diverse plant group on the Earth. Leaves of angiosperms can be grouped as monocots or dicots based on their shape and venation. Different plant groups present different ways of solving problems, each with advantages and challenges or exceptions for survival.

concepts.label: Kingdom Animalia and the Notochord
concepts.cardText: Animals are multicellular and heterotrophic organisms that depend on other organisms for their food. Most animals exhibit locomotion, rapid response to stimuli and coordinated behaviour, which allow them to actively search for food, avoid predators and interact dynamically with their surroundings. One of the major criteria for classifying animals is the presence or absence of a notochord, a flexible rod-shaped structure. Based on its absence or presence animals are classified into two groups: non-chordata (invertebrata) and chordata. In some chordates the notochord acts as a precursor for the development of the vertebral column. The chordata is further classified as protochordata and vertebrata. Invertebrates lack a notochord yet show a wide range of body organisation, from a simple structure to complex organ systems.

concepts.label: Porifera and Cnidaria
concepts.cardText: Sponges (Porifera, pore-bearers) represent one of the simplest animal body plans: they are multicellular but lack organisation of tissues and organs. Numerous pores in their body allow water to flow continuously through it, bringing food particles and oxygen directly to individual cells and carrying waste away. Sponges remain fixed in one place and are found in aquatic environments. Cnidarians, such as Hydra, jellyfish and corals, show a major change in body organisation: tissue-level organisation is present in them, which allows specialised cells to perform specific functions, such as the tentacles used for capturing prey. Unlike poriferans, cnidarians can catch their prey using tentacles instead of depending on water currents to bring food particles in through pores. However, cnidarians have a single opening that functions for both food intake and waste removal.

concepts.label: Platyhelminthes and Nematoda
concepts.cardText: Flatworms (Platyhelminthes) show organisational advancement through bilateral symmetry, in which the organism's body can be divided into two halves along one plane and the body has distinct head-tail and front-back regions. This allows better coordination of movement and is the beginning of directional activity. Their flattened bodies permit efficient diffusion of gases without specialised respiratory organs, but there is still a single opening for food intake and waste elimination. Many flatworms have adopted a parasitic lifestyle, with hooks and suckers to attach firmly to host tissues for obtaining nutrients. Infectious diseases caused by parasitic worms enter the body through contaminated water and food, so one should wash hands properly, maintain personal hygiene and good sanitary habits, and consume properly cooked food and boiled or filtered drinking water. Roundworms (Nematoda) have elongated, cylindrical bodies that allow efficient movement through soil, water or host tissues, and two openings, a mouth and an anus.

concepts.label: Annelida and Arthropoda
concepts.cardText: Annelids, such as earthworms, represent a notable development in body organisation: their bodies are cylindrical and divided into segments. They possess organ system level of organisation, with muscles that help in locomotion and a nerve cord that helps in control and coordination. Segmentation allows greater flexibility and more precise control of movements, and a body cavity is also present. Arthropods (arthro means limbs and poda means appendages) include insects, crabs and spiders. They have segmented bodies with different segments specialised for different functions. A defining structural feature of arthropods is the development of a hard external skeleton. This outer covering provides protection, reduces water loss and supports powerful muscles, allowing arthropods to survive in dry and exposed environments.

concepts.label: Mollusca and Echinodermata
concepts.cardText: Molluscs, such as snails, squids and octopuses, show organ system level organisation with soft bodies; in many molluscs the development of a shell provides protection to these soft bodies. Echinoderms (echinos means spiny and derma means skin), such as starfish and sea urchins, possess a hard internal skeleton made of calcium carbonate. Although they lack a notochord, this internal skeleton provides them protection and controlled movement, and their body organisation is quite like that of more complex animals, showing a gradual shift towards internal skeletal support. From sponges to echinoderms, animal body structure shows a pattern of increasing complexity in body organisation; new structural features improve feeding, movement and protection but often introduce new challenges.

concepts.label: Protochordates and Vertebrates
concepts.cardText: Protochordates, like Amphioxus, possess a notochord at least once during their life. This structure provides internal support without restricting movement and represents a crucial change in body organisation; protochordates are a primitive type of chordates that help us understand how animals with a notochord may have arisen from simpler forms. Vertebrates possess a vertebral column (backbone), an internal skeletal structure that supports the body and protects vital organs such as the brain and the spinal cord. This internal framework allows a larger body size, efficient movement and the development of complex organ systems, and vertebrates show advanced sensory abilities and coordinated behaviour. Vertebrates are classified into five groups, namely fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals, based on the broad patterns of their habitat use, body covering and reproduction.

concepts.label: Adaptations as Outcomes of Structural Change
concepts.cardText: The diversity seen in animals today is an outcome of changes in body structure over long periods of time. Fins and gills allow fish to move and breathe in water. Feathers and hollow bones make flight possible in birds. Fat storage in camels and thick fur in polar bears illustrate how structural features support survival under extreme conditions. In mammals, mammary glands represent an additional structural and functional change that improves the survival of young ones. These features are interconnected and reflect how different vertebrates tackle the challenges of survival in different environments. Forests with rich biodiversity can also work as barriers: villages with more mangroves experienced less destruction in the 1999 super cyclone in Orissa.

concepts.label: The Hierarchical Nature of Classification
concepts.cardText: Classification follows a step-by-step order, starting from very broad groups and moving towards smaller and more specific ones: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species. At each lower level, organisms share more common features, and every lower group is a part of the group above it. This arrangement works like an address: just as a house address helps us locate a place exactly, classification helps scientists identify, compare and study organisms accurately, and understand how they are related.

concepts.label: Binomial Nomenclature
concepts.cardText: A tiger is called bagh in Hindi, puli in Tamil, tiger in English and tigre in French, and confusion may arise if people from different regions discuss the animal. To avoid this, scientists use a universal system of naming living organisms called binomial nomenclature, introduced by Carolus Linnaeus in the 18th century. According to this, every organism has a scientific name with two parts, written in Latin or a Latinised form. The first word, such as Panthera or Mangifera, is the name of the genus and the second, such as tigris or indica, is the name of the species. A genus groups closely related species that share common features, as Panthera tigris (tiger) and Panthera leo (lion) under the genus Panthera, the roaring cats. The species name indicates a group of similar individuals capable of interbreeding and producing offspring. Together the genus and species name form a unique scientific name used worldwide. The rules: the name has two parts, genus and species; the genus name begins with a capital letter and comes first, followed by the species name in small letters; and the scientific name is written in italics when printed or underlined when handwritten.

concepts.label: Three Domains and the Changing Nature of Classification
concepts.cardText: With advances in microscopes and genetic studies, scientists began to compare organisms at the DNA level. Every living cell contains genetic material (DNA), which carries the instructions for its growth and function, and organisms with similar DNA are considered to have a common ancestry. Based on genetic data, Carl Woese in 1977 proposed the three domain system: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya, showing that microscopic life forms are far more diverse than previously believed. Classification systems keep changing because science evolves and progresses as we learn new things: Aristotle's system worked for his time, but new tools like microscopes and staining techniques revealed microorganisms, so the biological classification changed. Classification, and science, is thus an ongoing process of reasoning and change.

concepts.label: Fossils as Evidence
concepts.cardText: Fossils are preserved remains of plants and animals found in layers of rocks, sand and mud. Generally older layers contain simpler organisms, while newer layers show more complex forms. From giant dinosaurs to early humans and ancient plants, some important fossils have been discovered in India. Fossils act as natural records that help us understand how life has changed over millions of years. Birbal Sahni studied fossil plants and founded the Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences in Lucknow; his studies helped link present-day plants with their ancestors and showed that life on the Earth has a long, connected history.

concepts.label: Biodiversity Under Threat
concepts.cardText: Each species, large or small, plays an important role in nature: plants produce food and oxygen, animals pollinate flowers and disperse seeds, and microorganisms recycle nutrients. Human activities such as pollution, deforestation, the overuse of resources and climate change are reducing biodiversity. When one species disappears, others that depend on it may also decline in number and eventually disappear. The floating grasslands called phumdis in Loktak lake, Manipur, are a unique habitat of the endemic Sangai deer, which was declared extinct in 1951 and rediscovered in 1953; recently the phumdis are degenerating and the Sangai is listed in the IUCN Red Data list, and habitat loss will significantly affect its population.
